newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. Haiti mission extended final time for 8 months.
newsitem.headline: U.N. Haiti mission extended final time for 8 months.

text.p: The Security Council on Thursday renewed the U.N. peacekeeping mission in Haiti for a maximum of eight months before it is shut down entirely at the insistence of Russia and China.
In a 15-0 vote, the council agreed to extend the mission until May 31, subject to renewal for another two months until July 31, as Haiti's President Rene Preval had requested.
There are 1,300 troops and close to 300 civilian police in Haiti. Half of the troops are financed by Canada and the United States rather than by all U.N. members.
The new resolution cut the number of troops by 100 but Canada said it would continue to finance the same number of its own contingents and keep them at the same level.

Neither the United States nor Canada wanted to decide at this point whether all troops and police should leave in July but they probably would have faced a veto by Russia and China had they not agreed on a final extension, diplomats said.

Canadian Ambassador Robert Fowler said he believed Haiti would be able to manage the transition but the country would continue to need help, especially economic assistance. But he did not say whether Canada would continue fielding some troops or police monitors after the U.N. mandate ended.

U.S. envoy Karl Inderfurth said while progress was considerable there continued to be groups opposing democracy in Haiti. "The day is approaching when the government of Haiti will be able to assume full responsibility for public safety, but that day has not yet arrived."

One of the operation's main tasks is to train and monitor Haiti's fledgling police, which replaced the previous paramilitary contingents loyal to the military junta that overthrew elected President Jean-Bertrand Aristide in 1991.

He was restored to power three years later by a U.S.-led 22,000-member multinational force. The United Nations took over peacekeeping in March 1995 with 6,000 troops, a number that has been steadily reduced since then.

In advocating the current renewal be the final one, Russian envoy Yuri Fedotov said: "It is our profound conviction that the situation in this country does not represent a threat to international or even regional peace and security."

Russia frequently objected to keeping U.N. peacekeepers in the U.S. sphere of influence when the council rejected similar requests for troops in the former Soviet republics of Georgia and Tajikistan and some hot spots in the rest of the world.
Fedotov again said the entire mission reflected a "manifestation of double standards" when there were other crises in the world that required attention.

China's Ambassador Qin Huasun said his country supported the peace process in Haiti but "under the current circumstances the U.N. peacekeeping mission is over. The main task is economic construction."

China has a history of challenging the entire operation because of Haiti's ties with Taiwan, which it considers a renegade province, despite a marked improvement in relations between Beijing and the impoverished Caribbean nation.

Last February China threatened to veto the military force in Haiti unless its numbers were reduced, prompting Canada to rescue the mission by paying for its own troops for six months. In June, the United States as well as Canada helped pay for the Canadian and Pakistani troops.
